title: Acute hypotension
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: For new low blood pressure plus altered mental status, assess the patient immediately and call for urgent help in parallel, not after several observation rounds.
Recognise abnormal mentation, capillary refill, skin temperature and urine output as perfusion concerns requiring urgent team assessment; no single reading proves shock subtype.
Review infusions and recent medicines that could be contributing and tell the prescriber.
Leave fluids and vasopressor changes to the prescriber and protocol.

sources.use: Open RN Nursing Fundamentals 15.6: hypotension with a fast, weak pulse as hallmark of fluid volume deficit; urine output; impending shock needs emergent care
ESICM consensus (2014, dated): shock recognition and monitoring items

required_sources: Independent nursing/medical review of full ESICM 2025 shock evidence and local emergency response policy; publisher commercial reuse clearance if needed

gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Causes and treatment of hypotension are not drawn from a full guideline; the scenario keeps to assessment, review of infusions, escalation and monitoring.

Measurement-quality principles are mapped to SK-01, a 2025 discordance review abstract and a 2023 meta-analysis abstract; the 2025 EVERDAC trial is contextual evidence on a selective monitoring strategy, not individual measurement accuracy.
Numeric reporting thresholds in the Open RN text are generic and are not written.

Selected ESICM 2025 fluid-responsiveness recommendations checked in extracted PDF text; visual inspection unavailable and complete guideline remains unappraised. Publisher reuse restricted and independent clinical validation remains required.

setting: A fictional adult in a fictional intensive care unit with a drain and a recent episode of diarrhoea, on routine infusions.

steps.info: A low-pressure alarm sounds during ICU monitoring. The adult is slower to respond than an hour earlier and the heart rate is faster. The pressure signal has not yet been verified, but the change in alertness is clinically apparent.
steps.prompt: How should the nurse assess new hypotension while checking whether the measurement is reliable?

observations.label: Pressure signal
observations.value: Verify in parallel with clinical assessment

options.text: Assess airway, breathing and perfusion immediately; activate urgent clinical help now. Ask a colleague to verify pressure, repeat readings and review infusions while you remain with the patient.
options.feedback: Altered responsiveness plus hypotension is a potentially unstable presentation. Patient-first ABC/perfusion assessment and immediate clinical escalation must happen together with checking a measurement for error, not after repeated observation. The ESICM 2025 summary emphasizes serial clinical perfusion assessment; diagnosis and treatment remain team-led. The 2025 ESICM guideline supports arterial catheter monitoring for shock unresponsive to initial treatment or requiring vasopressors. If an arterial reading is implausible, check the patient and waveform, transducer reference level and equipment with a trained colleague; compare with another appropriate measurement in parallel, not as a condition for escalation. The 2025 EVERDAC trial found a monitored cuff-first strategy with predefined rescue criteria noninferior for 28-day mortality in its selected shock population. This does not establish that cuff and arterial readings are interchangeable or justify removal of a functioning line. For discrepant readings, check cuff fit and position, arterial waveform and reference level, and report perfusion findings to the responsible team. Do not average the two readings or choose whichever looks more reassuring.
options.consequence: Urgent clinical assessment with parallel signal verification may identify circulatory deterioration without delaying emergency help.

options.text: Treat the low-pressure alarm as a likely measurement error, silence it and document the earlier readings and current heart rate; defer the next blood-pressure check and bedside assessment to the routine round.
options.feedback: A fall in pressure with a faster pulse and altered mental state must be assessed at the bedside and cannot be dismissed as artefact.
options.consequence: Dismissing the reading as artefact could delay recognition of genuine shock.

options.text: Assume the falling pressure reflects a fluid deficit and give a bolus from ward stock without an order or authorised pathway; obtain repeat readings and call for assessment only after the bolus.
options.feedback: Do not give an unauthorised bolus. Assess the patient and summon urgent clinical help; administer fluids only under an appropriate order or authorised protocol.
options.consequence: An unauthorized fluid bolus before assessment could worsen an unrecognized cause of hypotension.

steps.info: At the next shared checkpoint, pulse is fast and weak, skin is cool and urine output remains low. Drain and stool losses have been substantial during the shift. A prescribed vasopressor is running; the cause of poor perfusion and response to further fluid remain uncertain.
steps.prompt: Which reassessment and communication would help the team distinguish possible causes and direct resuscitation?

options.text: Update the responding team urgently: BP, pulse, mental state, capillary refill, skin, urine, losses, vasopressors and access. Continue assessment and ordered or protocol-authorised care.
options.feedback: Rapid trending and communication of tissue perfusion, losses and drug-delivery concerns help the responsible team determine the cause and safely direct resuscitation. Blood loss and diarrhoea are possible contributors, not sufficient evidence to diagnose only hypovolaemia. The ESICM update favors dynamic assessment of fluid responsiveness over static preload markers when applicable. A low pressure or a single filling-pressure value does not independently justify further fluid administration. For persistent shock after initial resuscitation, the team should assess likely fluid responsiveness before giving more fluid. Passive leg raising with measurement of the change in cardiac output or stroke volume can be useful even during spontaneous breathing. Pulse-pressure or stroke-volume variation is less reliable outside suitable controlled ventilation conditions; respiratory variation of inferior vena cava size alone is insufficient. Fluid responsiveness is not itself an indication for fluid: consider ongoing perfusion deficit and congestion with the treating team. Do not alter ventilator settings or perform a haemodynamic manoeuvre outside the authorised protocol.
options.consequence: Reporting losses, perfusion, medication delivery and access findings may support individualized assessment of shock and fluid needs.

options.text: Review the current vasopressor rate and raise it independently until pressure improves, then communicate the new reading to the team without first reporting the ongoing perfusion findings or access concerns.
options.feedback: Vasopressor changes are made as prescribed or per the unit's titration protocol; the label notes risks including slowed heart rate and infusion-site injury.
options.consequence: An unauthorized infusion increase could worsen adverse effects while the underlying cause remains unresolved.

options.text: Reassure the family that the change in alertness reflects tiredness, record the losses and urine output for the next handover, and continue routine care without reporting the new perfusion concerns urgently.
options.feedback: These findings suggest possible shock and need urgent reporting, not reassurance.
options.consequence: Routine reassurance could delay urgent review of deteriorating perfusion.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint, the urgent response has been activated but the team is not yet at the bedside. Pressure remains low, skin is cold and clammy and the patient is newly confused. The previous call has not resolved the emergency.
steps.prompt: What should the bedside nurse do when severe perfusion concerns persist while awaiting help?

options.text: Escalate again through the emergency chain, stay with the patient, reassess ABC and perfusion trends, and coordinate the urgent team's authorised care.
options.feedback: Ongoing confusion, poor perfusion and hypotension after a previous urgent call need repeated escalation and continuous reassessment, not silence or waiting for a routine review.
options.consequence: Repeated escalation through the emergency chain and ongoing reassessment may shorten delay to appropriate treatment.

options.text: Continue repeating blood-pressure readings and recording the results for a few more minutes, delaying a further emergency call until the trend is clearer despite the new confusion and cold skin.
options.feedback: Monitoring continues, but waiting to escalate a patient with signs of impending shock delays emergency care.
options.consequence: Repeated pressure checks alone could delay escalation while organ perfusion worsens.

options.text: Sit the patient upright to improve breathing, leave the bedside to find a doctor and report the earlier pressure readings when you locate the team, then return to reassess the patient.
options.feedback: The patient should not be left alone, and positioning should follow the clinical situation and policy; escalate while staying with the patient.
options.consequence: Leaving the patient could interrupt observation and immediate support during deterioration.

learning_points: Altered mentation with a new low blood pressure requires immediate patient assessment and urgent team activation; measurement verification and infusion checks proceed in parallel, never as reasons to delay help.

Use changing perfusion signs (mental status, skin and capillary refill, pulse, urine output) and source losses in a structured handover; do not infer a shock subtype solely from a fast pulse or one pressure value.
Review infusions and recent medicines, including infusion sites, and tell the prescriber.
Do not change vasopressors or give fluids on your own; report with SBAR and escalate early.
Use the clinician-directed monitoring plan and check arterial measurement quality when readings are implausible; fluid responsiveness assessment and resuscitation decisions require clinical context.
A selective cuff-first strategy is not equivalent to assuming all invasive and noninvasive readings agree; escalate discordance using clinical perfusion and technical checks.
Fluid responsiveness testing has method-specific limitations; a positive response alone is not an instruction to administer fluid. Report congestion and the clinical perfusion trajectory.
